Tides are the rhythmic rise and fall of ocean levels, a phenomenon primarily driven by the gravitational interactions between the Earth, the Moon, and the Sun. While the Sun is much larger, the Moon’s proximity to Earth makes its gravitational influence on the oceans significantly stronger. As the Moon orbits our planet, its gravity pulls on the Earth and its waters. This force is strongest on the side of the Earth facing the Moon, drawing the ocean water toward it and creating a bulge. Simultaneously, on the opposite side of the Earth, centrifugal force generated by the Earth-Moon system's rotation creates a second bulge. These two high tides remain relatively stationary as the Earth rotates beneath them, meaning most coastal areas experience two high tides and two low tides each day.

However, the Sun also exerts a gravitational pull on Earth’s oceans, though its effect is roughly half that of the Moon’s. When the Sun, Moon, and Earth align during new and full moons, their gravitational forces combine to produce higher high tides and lower low tides, known as spring tides. Conversely, during the first and third quarters of the moon, the Sun and Moon are at right angles relative to Earth, causing their gravitational forces to partially cancel each other out. This results in neap tides, where the difference between high and low water levels is minimized. Local geography plays a crucial role as well; the shape of coastlines, the depth of the ocean floor, and the rotation of the Earth influence how tidal waves move and amplify. Friction with the ocean floor and the Coriolis effect further complicate tidal patterns, creating unique tidal behaviors in different regions around the globe. Ultimately, tides are a complex interplay of celestial mechanics and terrestrial geography, constantly shaping the coastal environment.
